newsitem.title: USA: Bankers' lawyers say fraud case is set up.
newsitem.headline: Bankers' lawyers say fraud case is set up.

text.p: Lawyers for Cuban-born banker Orlando Castro Llanes, his son and grandson reiterated on Friday that a bank fraud charge against them was revenge by the Venezuelan government.

Castro Llanes, his son Orlando Castro and grandson Castro Barredo, were accused of illegally using deposits in a family controlled bank, Banco Progreso International de Puerto Rico (BPIPR), to prop up financial institutions they controlled in Central and South America.

The case was being tried in New York because prosecutors claimed money was transferred through New York banks, including two multimillion-dollar transfers. The issue of jurisdiction will ultimately be decided by the jury.

"What you'll hear is evidence that every single depositor, banker, stockbroker and conversation ... was made outside the United States," said Marc Nurik, attorney for Castro Barredo in opening statements in Manhattan Supreme Court.
His statement echoed that of Richard Sharpstein, the lawyer for Castro Llanes. He argued on Thursday that his client was set up by the Venezuelan government, who considers him "a political enemy."
"You will find insufficent proof of any crime in New York," Nurik also told the jury.

The 12 jurors hearing the complicated financial case include a retired union member, two nurses, an actor and an unemployed parking attendant. More than one juror dozed off during the attorneys' presentations.
The prosecution's first witness, a Fordham University economics professor, was expected to give jurors an overview of banking.
The prosecution contends the three men misled Venezuelan depositors to believe BPIPR was a safe offshore bank subject to tight regulatory control, attracting deposits of more than $55 million.
BPIPR closed in January 1995 with uninsured loses to depositors of more than $15 million.

Until the eldest Castro was forced to flee Venezuela in 1994 he oversaw a small empire that included 40 radio stations, four insurance firms, car rental companies and coffee manufacturing plants, his attorney said.
